\2. Recent Economic Developments in Kosovo The previous year (2022) was characterized by a sustainable economic growth of 5.2% in real terms and 12.3% in nominal terms, while inflation marked an average rate of 11.6%.

According to the data from ASK, the growth of economic activity continued in the first part of 2023. This growth was predominantly driven by consumption, which rose by 2.2% in real terms, contributing 2.3 percentage points to GDP growth.

Inflation- Harmonized consumer price index increased in average 5.8% in the period JanuarySeptember 2023, reflecting a pronounced downward trend (it decreased from an average rate of

11.6% in January to 4.2% in September). The categories witnessing the most significant hikes were: 'food and non-alcoholic beverages' at an increase of 10.3%, 'supply, household appliances, and routine home maintenance' at 8.2%, and 'housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels' at

7.3%. Meanwhile, the 'transport' category experienced a decline of 2.0%, mirroring the decline in international oil prices during this period.

In the first half of 2023, total investments (both private and public) rose by 1.6% compared to the same period in 2022, contributing positively to GDP growth by 0.6 percentage points, considerably due to the base effect.

Net exports in the first six months of 2023 maintained a similar level as in the same period last year. While goods exports saw a real decline of 6.6%, negatively impacting the GDP by 0.8 percentage points, service exports surged by 18.3% in real terms, positively contributing to the GDP growth by 4.0 percentage points.

The import of goods grew by 1.6%, contributing negatively by 1 percentage point to the GDP, and service imports increased by 19.7%, contributing by 2.3 percentage points.

During the period from January to July, the current account deficit reached a value of -450.2 million euros, a significant reduction by approximately 23.0% compared to the same period the previous year.

Trade in goods during 2023 reflected the effects of price increases. The goods trade deficit continued to grow during this time, expanding by around 3.8%. Conversely, the service surplus noted an annual rise of 24.9%.

The export of goods recorded a decrease of 6.2%, while the export of services recorded an annual increase of 20.7%.

According to the latest data on the goods export structure, there was a decrease on the share of the export of other manufactured items in the total export (13.2% from 21.4% in the previous year);

decrease in the share of the category "base metals and articles thereof" to 20.8% of total exports, and the category "plastics, tires and articles" with a share of 13.4%. As for the contribution of the categories to the decrease in the export of goods, the export of other manufactured articles had a

more pronounced impact with 9.0 p.p., basic metals and articles thereof with 6.1 p.p., and plastics, rubber and articles thereof with 1.4 p.p. The impressive 20.7% increase in service exports from the same period last year was predominantly driven by growth in travel services, which contributed

12.6 p.p. Other significant contributors included computer, information, and telecommunication services at 4.2 p.p., and other business services at 1.8 p.p.

The import of goods recorded a rise of 2.0% compared to the previous year. This increase was mainly attributed to the 'means of transport' category with a contribution of 3.1 p.p., textiles and their articles contributing 1.6 p.p., and machinery, tools, and electrical equipment adding 1.1 p.p.

However, this was countered by a negative contribution from the 'mineral products' category at 4.4 p.p., and the plastics, rubber, and related items category which detracted 1.3 p.p. Meanwhile, the import of services recorded an increase of 16.1%, driven mainly by a marked increase in the import of travel services with a contribution of 14.1 p.p., and the category computer information and telecommunication services with 2.9 p.p.

The balance of primary income during the period January-July 2023 decreased by 24.6% compared to the same period in the previous year, meanwhile, the balance from secondary income saw an annual rise of 7.4% for the same period.

Bank credit has continued to be a stable source of financing for the economy. At the end of August 2023, the stock of loans reached the value of about 4.7 billion euros, marking an increase of 13.2% compared to the previous year. The stock of corporate loans increased by 11.1%, while the stock of household loans increased by

16.9%.

Deposits continued to grow, with the main contribution from households. At the end of August 2023, the stock of total deposits reached the value of about 5.8 billion euros, marking an annual increase of 12.2%. The stock of corporate deposits increased by 17.6%, while that of households increased by 9.8%. As for the type of deposits, transferable deposits recorded an annual increase of 6.6% and contributed to the increase of total deposits by 4.4 p.p.

The level of non-performing loans (NPL) reached 2.0% at the end of August 2023 marking a slight improvement from the same period last year. The average weighted interest rate of loans during the period January-August 2023 was 6.7%, or by about 0.7 p.p. higher than in the same period last year. Meanwhile, the weighted average interest rate on deposits fluctuated around 2.5%, from

1.8%, which was the average during the same period last year.

\3. Macroeconomic perspective According to MFLT assessments, Kosovo’s economy during the current year is expected to grow by around 3.9% in real terms and 9.6% in nominal terms. The latest KAS data, indicates that Kosovo's economy has continued its growth trend.

The expectation for an average real economic growth of 3.9% in 2023 shows a downward revision of about 1.3 percentage points compared to the previous round of projections carried out in April 2023. This is mainly a result of the downward revision of the contribution of total investments (from a positive contribution of 1.9 p.p to a slight contribution of 0.1 p.p) due to increased uncertainty from high inflationary pressures, slower execution of capital expenditures, and the increase in loan interest rates. In contrast, the contribution of the export of goods and services has been upward revised by 0.7 p.p. (from 1.6 p.p to 2.3 p.p).

Considering a moderate growth during the current year, the economy of Kosovo is expected to grow at a faster rate in the next year (2024), estimated at 4.6% in real terms and 7.8% in nominal terms.

Unlike 2023, the main contribution to economic growth in 2024 is anticipated from investments (both private and public). Public investments are projected to see a quicker pace of execution due to both new projects and the continuation of existing projects- implementation of which is expected to accelerate. Furthermore, private investments are forecasted to boost, bolstered by reduced uncertainty in the country, a series of fiscal stimulus policies targeting the private sector, and the improvement of private sector balance sheets.

The continuation of the upward trend of bank credit combined with a series of social transfers within the 'Economic Recovery Package'3 framework for family support will continue to support the growth of private consumption in the coming year, while remittances will continue to grow, although at a slower pace than in previous years. Regarding to the public consumption, it will increase due to the rise in the wage coefficient in the public sector foreseen by the law and the implementation of some regulations for additional benefits deriving from the law on wages in the public sector, as well as the increase in expenditure for government goods and services.

The export of goods and services will continue positive contribution to almost the same extent as the previous year (with differences between the contribution of goods and that of services), mainly due to the base effect, the increase in the export of goods, and the stabilization of basic goods prices in international markets.

The import of goods and services will continue its upward trend, where among the main factors for this increase is the rise in capital investments.

The Consumer Price Index is expected to fluctuate around 5.1% during 2023, which is significantly lower than the level recorded in 2022 (11.6%). The inflation trend has been shaped by international developments in the prices of food, energy, and oil markets, stemming from the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine and geopolitical tensions.

During the next year (2024), based on projections for commodity prices in international markets, inflation in Kosovo is expected to drop to 2.7% and is anticipated to further stabilize around an average of 2.3% in the medium term.

However, the projections for underlying inflation and economic growth are faced with heightened downside risks. These risks include significant spikes in core prices in international markets, pronounced economic downturns in trading partners, and further developments in Kosovo's energy sector.

\4. Government revenues and expenditure

4.1 Revenues and expenditures January-September 2023 The data for the period January-September 2023 indicates that budget revenues and expenditure increased compared to the same period of the last year. More specifically, budget revenues (including DDG-s) amounted to 2,114.7 million Euros, marking an increase by 14.3% compared to the same period of 2022. On the other hand, budget expenditure (including DDGs) amounted to 1,826.3 million Euros increasing by 15.2%. However, revenues achieved a higher rate of realization than expenditures compared to projections at the beginning of the year. Considering the flow of revenues and expenditure, the total budget balance recorded a surplus of 288.4 million Euros for this period.

Direct tax revenues increased by approximately 19.8%in annual terms for the period JanuarySeptember 2023, amounting to 376.1 million Euros. This increase was, among others, a result of the growth in the number of employees in the private sector. Examining the categories of direct revenues: revenues from personal income tax rose by about 19.3% compared to the previous period, while corporate income tax grew by 15.6%. It is worth noting that the property tax, due to the revaluation of properties, saw the largest growth among the categories of direct taxes, with an increase rate of 46.8%.

Indirect tax revenues have shown a significant increase, largely due to the growth in the value of goods imports. Customs data reveals that for the period January-September 2023, regular imports grew by 2.5%. During this period, indirect tax revenues rose by 9.4% compared to JanuarySeptember 2022, totaling 1,506.7 million Euros. While revenues from customs duty increased at an annual rate by 15.7%, the annual growth of revenues from border VAT was 6.5% for the period January-September 2023. Excise duty, one of the major contributor to indirect revenues, also followed an upward trajectory, increasing at a rate of 5.5% for the reporting period.

During this period, non-tax revenues amounted to 197.4 million Euros, marking an increase of

4.2% in annual terms. The most significant growth within the non-tax revenue categories came from the concessionary tax, which rose by approximately 39.3%, attributed to the growing number of passengers at Pristina International Airport. Analyzing non-tax revenues by government level reveals that the local level experienced an increase of 19.1%, while the central level saw a decrease of 3.0% in non-tax revenues.

Regarding budget expenditure, all categories contributed positively to the growth of total expenditure for the period January-September 2023. The category of wages and salaries recorded an annual increase of 18.5% compared to last year, a result of implementing the new law on public sector wages from February 2023. Expenditure for goods and services also saw a double-digit rise

(17.7%), amounting to 257.2 million Euros, which is 38.8 million Euros more than in the same period of 2022 On the other hand subsidies and transfers were not characterized by any significant movement compared to the same period of 2022. This is due to the high growth in the past year and the

implementation of the measures of the economic recovery package, which continued to be implemented for the January-September 2023 period as well. For this reporting period, the expenditure structure of the recovery package remained dominated by the category of subsidies and transfers.

Capital expenditure for the period January-September 2023 saw a significant increase by 66.9% compared to the same period of 2022. It is worth noting that part of this increase can be attributed to the base effect, since in the same period of 2022, capital expenditure had decreased by about

28.7%. As for the financing structure of capital expenditures for the period January-September 2023, the regular budget dominated with about 82.6%, to be followed by own revenues (13.6%), external borrowing financed by the investment clause (3.2%), and regular external borrowing

(0.7%).

Interest expenditure during the period January-September amounted to 32.9 million euros, marking an annual increase of 21.0%.

4.2 Forecast of revenues for 2024 and mid-term period Budget revenues for the medium-term period are expected to increase by about 5.7%, mainly due to the continuation of government measures, voluntary compliance, and the formalization of the economy.

Indirect tax revenues are projected to constitute around 74.3% of total revenues in 2024 and are expected to see an increase of approximately 7.3% compared to the 2023 Budget.

Direct tax revenues in 2024 are anticipated to rise by about 6.0% compared to the 2023 Amended Budget, making up 17.7% of total revenues.

Non-tax revenues during 2024 are expected to increase by 12.1% compared to the 2023 Amended Budget Law, totaling about 292.9 million Euros.

Grants in 2024 are projected to be 30.0 million Euros, representing a significant drop from the previous year. This decrease from last year is primarily due to a one-time EU grant received in 2023, which amounted to 67.5 million Euros to support the energy sector. In 2024, funding from the same grant will be 7.5 million Euros.

For the period 2025-2026, total budget revenues are projected to increase by an average of 6.1%.

During this period, direct taxes are anticipated to grow by an average of 5.7%; indirect taxes by an average of 6.6%; and non-tax revenues are expected to follow their historical trend, increasing on average by 4.8%.

4.3 Forecast of expenditure for the period 2024 and the mid-term period Total budget expenditures in 2024 are expected to increase by 2.3% in annual terms, compared to the Amended Budget for 2023.

Total Current Expenditures during 2024 are planned to have an increase of 1.6% compared to the Amended Budget for 2023, reaching the value of 2,396.8 million Euros.

Expenditures for the wage and salaries category are planned to be 805.4 million Euros and while not exceeding the fiscal rule, they're projected to increase by 8.0%. This growth is attributed to the rise in the wage coefficient and the implementation of certain regulations affecting public officials'

wages. Expenditures in the category of goods and services are planned to increase by 5.1% compared to the Amended Budget for 2023, as a result of new classifications. Subsidies and transfers in 2024 are expected to have a decrease of 3.5%. This drop is primarily due to the expenses related to the grant received from the EU to support the energy sector. Meanwhile, 10.2 million Euros have been allocated to the current reserve category.

In 2024, capital expenditure is projected to grow by 4.8%, accounting for 26.0% of total expenditure. During this period, the implementation of capital projects is expected based on a list of priorities that contains projects with an impact on the improvement of the transport network, the improvement of the electricity network and the improvement of conditions in education, social and health systems. While the majority of capital investments are anticipated to be financed from the regular budget, a significant number of projects across various sectors are planned to be funded through external borrowing via the investment clause.

4.3.1 Expenditure in central level 2024-2026 The budget allocated for the central level in 2024 is projected to see an increase of 0.3% compared to the 2023 Budget. Although the overall planned expenditures for 2024 remain nearly the same, there are variations in the category-wise allocations. The most significant increase is anticipated in the capital expenditure category at 6.1%. The goods and services category is also planned to rise at a rate of 4.3%. On the other side, the 'wages and salaries' category and the 'subsidies and transfers' category are forecasted to decrease by 1.6% and 3.8% respectively. The reduction in the 'wages and salaries' is attributed to the previous year's budgeting of a contingency for the Public Sector Wage Law under this category. The decline in the 'subsidies and transfers' is mainly due to the allocation of a grant from the EU in 2023, valued at 75 million euros, within this category.

Also, the value of the current reserve has increased to 9.8 million euros from the usual allocation of 4.8 million euros.

Budget deficit and fiscal rule As a result of the increased need for additional funding for the expenditure stemming from the economic recovery package, as well as the maintenance of the high participation of capital expenditures, the total budget deficit for 2024 is expected to be EUR 284.6 million, or about 2.7% of GDP, whereas the deficit according to the fiscal rule is expected to fluctuate at around 2% of

### GDP.

In the subsequent years (2025 and 2026), the budget deficit is forecasted to stay at roughly the same level, specifically to 2.0% in 2025, while in 2026 the budget deficit is expected to be 1.5% of GDP. As for the usable bank balance, it is expected to be at sufficient levels, approximately

2.8% of GDP in 2024; about 2.6% of GDP in 2025, and 2.7% in 2026.

\6. Financing and State debt During the period 2024-2026, the need for financing will continue to be covered primarily by external and internal borrowing. The Government of Kosovo has several sources of financing: (a)

borrowing from the internal market through securities, (b) receiving loans from international financial institutions. In 2023, no income from liquidation funds is expected. For 2024, the bank balance is projected to be around 2.8% of the projected GDP for that year. However, depending on the forecast and the collection of budget revenues and execution of expenditures throughout the budget year, the Minister of Finance, Labor, and Transfers may decide on a lower issuance of internal debt than the amount estimated in table 1 of this Law.

In the medium term, total debt, including state guarantees, is expected to reach 20.7% in 2024,

22.3% in 2025 and 23.2% in 2026.

\7. Fiscal Risks The macro-fiscal outlook for 2024 is subject to significant risks, predominantly from external sources. Given our economy's substantial interlinkages with international markets, especially through trade and remittances, vigilance is crucial.

Some of the main risks, categorized into external and internal, are detailed below.

### EXTERNAL RISKS

Unstable prices as a result of climate change and geopolitical developments.

Despite the slowdown in global price growth this year, uncertainties are still present. International institutions present three possible sources that could lead to price increases. First, climate change can cause a decrease in the production of cereals in different states (similarly to what happened last summer, due to the increase in temperatures and droughts in some countries, the production of cereals decreased). This may also happen in the future, causing an increase in food prices.

Second, the reduction of electricity production from fossil sources in order to protect the environment and the insufficient compensation from renewable energy sources can present shortages in production and thus affect the increase in energy prices. Third, the possibility of further intensification of the war in Ukraine and geopolitical tensions in other countries may bring new disruptions to the supply chain and may cause increases in the prices of food, oil, artificial fertilizers and other products. Given that inflation in our country is very sensitive to these international developments, all these risks mentioned above also apply to our country and bring uncertainty about price developments in the medium term. The other channel through which these international developments can affect economic activity in our country is through remittances from European countries. A potential surge in prices there would erode the real incomes of Kosovar immigrants, and in our country it would be reflected in a decrease in remittances, a decrease in travel services or a decrease in foreign direct investments.

Measures to address core inflation in the Eurozone The tightening monetary policies in the developed countries of the world were evaluated as successful in ensuring a decrease in inflation without causing large losses of economic activity.

Based on the latest IMF World Economic Outlook, these austerity measures should continue further to ensure that inflation approaches the target. Moreover, the persistence of core inflation is considered as a potential risk, which would further complicate the work of monetary policy to stabilize inflation, necessitating even tighter measures. Such measures could suppress economic activity. A decline in activity in countries where Kosovar immigrants reside could adversely affect their incomes and, by extension, Kosovo's economy. In this context, it is important to consider the many connections of our economy with that of other countries, especially through two main channels: trade and transfers of immigrants.

### INTERNAL RISKS

Internal crisis of energy Uncertainties surrounding international energy prices are mirrored in our country's internal energy situation. An increase in electricity consumption during winter could necessitate greater electricity imports. Furthermore, our aging production capacity might result in insufficient power generation, leading to significant power outages. Such disruptions could negatively impact production, and subsequently, investment and consumption, incurring additional fiscal costs. However, this risk is perceived to be lower now than in the past due to anticipated drops in international energy prices,

government initiatives to diversify energy production sources, and measures implemented for energy saving.

Fiscal risks from Public Enterprises An overview of Public Enterprise Sector In the Republic of Kosovo, there are two types of Public Enterprises (PE): those owned by the central government and those owned by the local government. At the central government level, the POE sector includes 19 enterprises, of which 17 are supervised by the Ministry of Economy;

KOSTT is supervised by the Assembly, while Gjakova Airport is supervised by the Kosovo Security Force (KSF). About 80 percent of Trepca is owned by the state, while 20 percent is owned by the employees. These POEs operate in several different sectors, such as: energy, transport, water supply, telecommunications and the mining sector. The following analysis was made based on the financial data belonging to 17 PEs supervised by the Ministry of Economy.

By the end of 2022, assets of the PE stood at 18.8% of GDP, marking a decrease of 0.9 percentage points from 19.7% in 2021. Liabilities also receded to 8.7% of GDP, down from 9.3% in 2021.

Total income of the PE sector surged to 6.4% of GDP, up from 5.5% in the previous year.

Overall, the PE sector reported a profit of 110 million euros in 2022, a remarkable turnaround from a loss of 5.3 million euros in 2021. This profit was solely attributed to the KEK's performance.

The sector's return on equity rebounded from a negative 1% in 2021 to 11% in 2022. Liquidity improved year-on-year, with the return on assets rising from 0% in 2021 to 6% in 2022.

Assessment of the fiscal risk of PE Economic and political factors, such as changes in tax policies, the impact of global crises, institutional inefficiency, the impact of international events, the increase in public debt can affect fiscal stability and present fiscal risks, which are factors that may lead to deviations in fiscal forecasts. Public Enterprises (PE) can have a direct influence on fiscal indicators. For instance, this might happen when there's a need for subsidies, credit, or capital (equity) investments that exceed expectations, when contingent obligations crystallize, or when tax and dividend incomes fall below projections. Additionally, PE can indirectly impact fiscal indicators through their effects on economic growth. When these enterprises are undercapitalized, unprofitable, or have low liquidity, the realization of risks in these entities becomes more likely to pose fiscal risks.

In 2022, the Government provided grants totaling 30 million euros to the Energy Corporation of Kosovo. This support aimed to cover the costs of imported electricity, ensuring the needs of end users were met.

Telecom of Kosovo received three loans, for liquidity obtained from the EBRD through the Government, loans for financing the package for voluntary dismissal of workers and loans for financing investment projects.

The infrastructure and equipment of the PE have notably depreciated, showing an imediate need for replacements. However, due to their poor financial standing, these enterprises cannot bear the costs associated with such investments. For entities like Public Railway Enterprises and Kosovo Post Telekom, the rates charged to consumers are set by regulatory bodies and these rates fall short of covering their operational costs.

Based on the audited annual statements for 2022, the fiscal risk assessment analysis was conducted for 18 PEs, where six main financial indicators were calculated for each company: i) cost coverage ratio; ii) return on capital; iii) the ratio of the fulfillment of short-term obligations with short-term assets; ('current ratio'), iv) days for the fulfillment of accounts receivable; v) ratio of debt to assets;

and vi) the ratio of debt to EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization). These indicators were chosen as they provide a comprehensive overview of the profitability, liquidity, and solvency of the PEs. Each indicator received a risk assessment based on international norm. The overall risk assessment is calculated as the arithmetic mean of the risk assessments for the individual reports.

Out of 18 Public Enterprises (PE), two were classified as "very high risk" (this is an increase from 2021 when only one PE fell into the "very high" risk category). The risk assessment reveals that, generally, the majority of PEs maintain a stable liquidity position. However, some are facing

challenges in collecting debts from their debtors. Moreover, many PEs shoulder high levels of debt, particularly concerning given their limited profitability to offset these liabilities.

To address the challenges previously mentioned, the Government is amending the Law on PEs, which governs the operations of the PE sector. The primary goal is to align the corporate governance of PEs with internationally recognized standards. This initiative is expected to boost the PEs' performance, enhance the value of their assets, and ensure the delivery of quality services to the public. In a related development, the Assembly of Kosovo has approved the draft law for the establishment of the Sovereign Fund. This institution is intended to manage public assets.

Another pressing issue is the stabilization of the boards and management of PEs. The government aims to achieve this through a transparent and merit-based process that might involve restructuring, privatization, or even liquidation.

Total liabilities

Cumulative distribution

Risk from contingent liabilities arising from sub-borrowed loans and government guarantees In Kosovo's state debt portfolio, the primary sources of potential risk are loans guaranteed for the public sector and international sub-loans to companies that provide essential public services. By the end of 2022, guaranteed loans amounted to 28.5 million euros, accounting for about 1.6% of the total debt. Particular attention needs to be given to the state guarantees for the PE “Trafiku Urban”. A significant deviation in the financial outcomes of these companies might burden the Government in the medium term, both in terms of subsidizing the services they offer and assuming financial obligations to external creditors.

To mitigate the impact of risks from contingent liabilities, the government will persist with measures such as: (a) monitoring the financial position of the beneficiaries (b) the initial

assessment of the possibility of the materialization of the existing contingent liabilities. Based on estimates of projected losses, guarantee fees will be set according to the Law on Public Debt.

Another risk management strategy includes factoring guarantees into the overall debt when calculating the debt-to-GDP ratio. In the medium-term plan, another proposed measure to manage these risks is the inclusion of a provision in the Budget Law that allocates funds for losses from guarantees in case of default by the primary borrower.

Fiscal risk from revenue collection A potential fiscal risk related to tax revenues is the ability to collect the receivable taxes. According to the annual financial report for 2022, uncollected receivable accounts are 841 million euros, 607 million euros of which related to the central government level and 232 million euros to the local government level. The total amount of 841 million euros of uncollected receivable accounts represents an increase of about 63 million euros compared to the previous year. The average annual growth for the period 2018-2022 reaches 7.5%.

Fiscal risks from court cases A key indicator of fiscal risks from litigation is the progress of annual government payments for court decisions. The following table presents the amount of payments according to court decisions for the past three years and the period until September 2023, including both the central and local levels. Until September 2023, most of the payments at the central level are related to the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure (accounting for 56.0% of the total payments from the central level) and the University Clinical Hospital Service of Kosovo (13.6% of the total payments from the central level). At the local level, municipalities such as Ferizaj, Pejë, Prishtina, and Prizren dominate these payments. Until September 2023, the expenses made based on court decisions accounted for 0.5% of the current expenses at the central level and 5.2% at the local level, cumulating to 1.6% of the total budget expenses. To better understand the fiscal risks arising from litigation, it's essential to consider the potential values that may arise from cases that are still in the court process.

Another potential source of fiscal risk is court cases from collective agreements. Collective agreements provide several benefits for public sector employees, such as food allowance payments, travel expenses, or additional payments after retirement. When public institutions fail to fulfill the obligations arising from these contracts, workers turn to the courts. These court decisions then represent additional costs for institutions, leading to an increase in unplanned expenses

Since this table is for informational purposes only, there may be changes compared to the existing tables in the pilot phase. The main differences compared to the existing table are:

\- Revenues are presented 'net'

\- Capital Transfers represent expenses that for the Government of Kosovo are current in nature (under the Subsidies & Transfers category) but represent capital investment (financial or non-financial) for the receiving public or non-public entity.

\- Capital Investments are disclosed according to sub-categories of the GFS, and they continue to be disclosed according to source funds in the following table for the calculation of the deficit and financing. There may be changes within the sub-categories, especially in the years after 2024, in the pilot phase of this table.
